claims.text: The powder feedstock is cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi intended for additive manufacturing.
The proposed intervention is powder-bed or substrate preheating during powder bed fusion.
A candidate preheating range is approximately 300–500 °C.
Laser energy density, scan strategy, and layer thickness are to be held constant when comparing preheated and room-temperature builds.
Powder-bed preheating produces a more uniform fabrication temperature profile.
A more uniform temperature profile reduces thermal gradients.
Reduced thermal gradients slow cooling rates.
Slower cooling mitigates rapid solute partitioning.
Preheating reduces the temperature differential between the melt pool and surrounding material.
The reduced temperature differential decreases residual thermal stress.
Preheating permits enhanced diffusion during solidification.
Enhanced diffusion during solidification yields a more homogeneous microstructure with less compositional segregation.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi builds will have lower residual stresses than room-temperature powder-bed-fusion builds.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi builds will have smaller compositional gradients than room-temperature powder-bed-fusion builds.
Preheated AlCrFeNiSi builds will exhibit improved tensile properties and hardness relative to room-temperature powder-bed-fusion builds.
The hypothesis is limited to powder bed fusion and may not apply to other fabrication techniques or substantially different preheating temperatures.
Preheating is known to reduce thermal gradients and residual stresses in many additively manufactured alloys.
The optimal preheating temperature and its effects on phase stability and microstructural evolution in AlCrFeNiSi remain experimentally unvalidated.
